summary:
Space Odyssey is an educational space mission simulation game for teenagers aged 15 to 18, created by Movimiento Naranja from Buenos Aires. NASA’s challenge was to build a game where players design, manage and simulate a complete space mission, and we set out to make it as realistic as possible.
Players choose between two missions, Mars or Saturn, and you can play alone. Each mission has three levels: designing the spacecraft and traveling, exploring and solving emergencies, and returning to Earth. Every decision about energy, propulsion, life support and communications has real consequences for the rest of the mission, and each one comes with a scientific explanation.
There are very few realistic space games, and educational,  almost none show what an astronaut’s work is really like. Space Odyssey fills that gap and teaches space engineering through play.
details: Space Odyssey is a simulation game where you can play alone or with your friends and take on a space mission to Mars or Saturn. The game has three levels. In the first level, you design your own rocket piece by piece. For each part, like the nose cone, you learn what it is for and what its characteristics are, and then you choose between different options. Then your rocket launches and travels to the planet you picked. In the second level, you solve the missions and emergencies that come up, like air leaks, power failures and communication blackouts. In the third level, you bring your crew back to Earth. The benefit is that players learn how a real space mission works by making decisions instead of memorizing, because every choice has consequences that carry through all three levels. Our intended impact is to clear up the misinformation about astronauts and show teenagers what their work is really like. We built it as a web game with React and TypeScript, and we used AI tools to help with the art and the code, with scientific information from NASA sources. It is creative because the whole mission is the lesson, and you can customize your own astronaut. As a team, we considered scientific accuracy, we labeled the missions as hypothetical, and we made it fun and challenging for ages 15 to 18.
